h.strategy: Use retrieved findings to classify settings as strong, weak, neutral or harmful, and to identify which settings can disconnect other parts from the outcome. Propose hypotheses only of two kinds. Self-conditioning: the edit's effect depends on the value it replaces, being more negative when that value is strong and more positive when it is empty or harmful. Disconnection: when the edited part cannot influence the outcome, its effect shrinks toward zero, so the direction is lower if the edit usually helps and higher if it usually hurts. Directions refer to the signed effect. For each hypothesis, state the edit's usual sign and a one-sentence mechanism. Cover varied edit fields and values. The critic should replace any hypothesis with an uncertain usual sign, competing effects or reliance on partial redundancy.

hyps.why: With edge 0 pruned node 1 is identically zero, so a conv on 1->3 contributes nothing and its usual gain vanishes.
With edge 5 pruned node 2 cannot reach the output, so a conv on 1->2 has no effect on the network.
If node 1 is already zero, edge 4 carries nothing, so pruning it costs nothing instead of its usual harm.
Pruning edge 4 is most harmful when it removes a strong 3x3 conv path directly into the output node.
Setting 0->3 to skip gains least, or loses, when it displaces a 3x3 conv that already adds capacity there.
Adding a residual on 0->3 helps most when no direct input-to-output path existed before.
A conv on 2->3 helps most when the edge was empty, since it reconnects the entire node-2 branch rather than just swapping an op.
Putting pooling on 1->2 hurts most when it replaces a 3x3 conv that carried learned features.
With edge 5 pruned node 2 is dead, so a conv on 0->2 cannot influence the output and its usual gain disappears.
With the deep path cut, the output relies only on edges 3 and 4, so removing the direct input path is far more damaging.
